concepts.title: Bharat and India: Names Across Time
concepts.definition: Our country has carried many names: Bharat, Bhāratavarsha and India, each rooted in ancient texts and usage, so that the constitution itself begins with the words, India, that is Bharat.
concepts.key_idea: Names hold memory: calling the land Bharat or India ties today's nation to millennia of history.

concepts.title: The Indian Subcontinent and Its Bounds
concepts.definition: India sits in the Indian subcontinent, a great triangle of land walled by the Himalayas in the north, washed by the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal, and crossed by rivers such as the Indus, Sarasvati and Ganga.
concepts.key_idea: Natural boundaries of mountains and seas helped a distinct civilisation grow between the Himalayas and the two seas.

concepts.title: Evidence from Sanchi Stupa
concepts.definition: A carving on the north gate of the Great Sanchi Stupa shows a rural Indian scene of about 2,300 years ago; monuments like Sanchi are material sources that let us picture life in ancient times.
concepts.key_idea: A stone carving is a window: the Sanchi panel preserves a day of village work from centuries ago.

concepts.title: India and Its Neighbours
concepts.definition: The chapter places India among its neighbours of the subcontinent and shows how land and sea routes linked the region, carrying goods and ideas in every direction for thousands of years.
concepts.key_idea: No country lives alone: India's story is tied to the lands and waters around it.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Why does the chapter show a carving from the Sanchi Stupa?

solution_template.explain: The north gate of the Great Sanchi Stupa carries a carved rural scene.
A carving 2,300 years old is evidence: it shows clothes, huts and work of that age without a single written word.

worked_examples.question_pattern: How do natural boundaries shape a civilisation?

solution_template.explain: Mountains in the north and seas on two sides fence the subcontinent.
Within this frame, rivers watered farms and routes joined people, letting one civilisation grow distinct.
